name: Bow drill
summary: Friction ignition from materials on the ground — the highest-effort, lowest-equipment way to an ember.
time: 1-3 hours to make the set, minutes to run it

materials.item: fireboard of the same or softer wood

steps.text: Everything must be BONE DRY. Damp wood makes dust that will not hold an ember, whatever your technique.
Carve a spindle about 20 cm long and thumb-thick — pointed at the top, blunt and rounded at the bottom.
steps.why: A narrow top point minimises friction where you do not want heat; a wide blunt base maximises it where you do.

steps.text: Burn a shallow socket into the fireboard with the spindle, then cut a V-notch from the edge into about one eighth of the socket, all the way through the board.
Set the ember pan under the notch. Load the spindle into the bowstring with one twist so it sits outside the string.
Kneel with your shin locked against your wrist, press down with the bearing block, and saw the full length of the bow, slow and long at first.
When black dust fills the notch and smoke rises on its own, give it ten fast hard strokes, then stop and do not move.
Let the dust pile smoke by itself, fan it gently, then tip it into the tinder bundle and blow it to flame.

verify: The dust is fine, black and powdery — brown, coarse dust means too little pressure or too slow a speed.
Smoke that continues rising for 10-20 seconds after you have stopped drilling is an ember.
limits: This is genuinely difficult and physically hard. Expect it to fail many times while you learn, which is a reason to learn it before you need it.
Wet weather, wet wood, or exhaustion beat it. It is the last resort, not the plan.
cautions: Blisters on your bearing hand will end your attempt — use a bearing block that actually spins freely, and grease the socket with anything oily.
Do not lean over the ember to blow it. Cup it and breathe steadily from the side.
